titre: Mare Liberum (1609): A Plea Before It Was a Principle
accroche: In 1603, the Dutch East India Company seizes a Portuguese carrack. Six years later, the pamphlet that defends the capture puts forward the idea of a free sea.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1603, off Singapore, three ships of the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, seize the *Santa Catarina*, a Portuguese carrack at anchor. Their commander, Jacob van Heemskerck, had received authorization to use force from neither the Company nor the government. The haul is considerable: the cargo includes 1,200 bales of raw Chinese silk, valued at 2.2 million guilders. Portugal demands its goods back, yet the Admiralty of Amsterdam decides to keep the ship and its cargo as a prize, and many see in the affair piracy barely disguised.

## A commission from the Company

Organized in 1602 by the Dutch government, the VOC is looking to win over public opinion. It turns to a 21-year-old jurist, Hugo Grotius, already renowned in Europe for his learning, but too new to the profession to have been hired to argue the case itself. He prepares a vast treatise on the law of prize, which will remain in his papers. Only one piece comes out of it: the twelfth chapter, reworked in 1608, appears in the spring of 1609 as a pamphlet, printed in Leiden by Elzevier. It does not bear its author's name. Its full title: *Mare liberum, sive de jure quod Batavis competit ad Indicana commercia dissertatio*, that is, “The Free Sea, or a Dissertation on the Right Which Belongs to the Dutch to Trade in the Indies.”

## What the pamphlet argues

Its target is precise: the Portuguese claim to reserve to the Portuguese alone navigation and trade to the East Indies. Grotius answers that a nation is free to travel to another and trade there, and that the sea, like the air, cannot be occupied by anyone: it is common to all. It is, as a first approximation, an argument against a particular monopoly.

## The shift

We like to present freedom of the seas as an idea that came out of legal reasoning alone. Its founding text is first of all a piece of defense, written for a company that had carried out the capture that needed justifying, against a rival whose monopoly it wanted to bring down. The treatise as a whole, of which the pamphlet is only one chapter, was not published until 1868 under the title *De jure praedae*, after a manuscript copy was discovered nearly three centuries later. The text we cite as a principle was therefore, originally, a chapter of advocacy. That says nothing about the value of the idea; what remains to be seen is what survives of a principle when the interest that gave it birth changes sides.

repere.texte: 1868: first complete publication of the treatise De jure praedae, of which Mare liberum (1609) is the twelfth chapter, the only one printed during Grotius's lifetime.
repere.source: Michael Widener, “Freedom of the Seas, Part 3,” Lillian Goldman Law Library, Yale Law School, October 22, 2009

carte.punch: Freedom of the seas began as a commissioned plea to justify a capture.
carte.idee: In 1609, the anonymous pamphlet Mare liberum asserts that the sea belongs to no one. It is the twelfth chapter of a treatise written to defend the 1603 seizure of a Portuguese carrack: a principle first formulated to serve a company's interest.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Freedom of the Seas, Part 3 (Yale Law Library)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A short account of the Company's commission and the publication of the 1609 pamphlet.

quiz.question: What was the immediate reason Grotius first wrote the argument for the free sea?
choix: To propose to the European states a treaty of common navigation on all the seas of the globe
To defend the seizure of a Portuguese cargo by the East India Company
To challenge before the States General the monopoly the Company was receiving over trade with the Indies
To argue before an international tribunal that Portugal had brought after the capture
quiz.explication: The chapter was born of a commission from the Company after the capture of the Santa Catarina in 1603: it defended a specific seizure. The text targets the Portuguese monopoly and defends the Company rather than challenging it; no source presents it as a project for a common navigation treaty, nor as a plea before an international tribunal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What share of the Santa Catarina's cargo do the 2.2 million guilders represent, according to the sources reopened?
choix: The value of the entire cargo, silk and other goods combined
The value of the 1,200 bales of raw Chinese silk only
The price the Dutch paid to buy the ship back from Portugal
The estimated value of the ship itself, without its cargo
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The sources specify that the 2.2 million guilders correspond to the value of the 1,200 bales of raw silk, not to that of the entire cargo or of the ship.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Grotius not argue the Santa Catarina case himself before the Dutch authorities?
choix: He was not yet 21 at the time of the seizure
He was already hired by Portugal as an adviser
He was too new to the profession to have been hired for that purpose
He refused to defend a prize he considered illegal
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Grotius, already renowned at 21, was according to the source too new to the profession to have been hired to argue the case himself before the authorities.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When was the complete treatise De jure praedae, of which Mare liberum is only one chapter, first published?
choix: In 1609, at the same time as Mare liberum
It was never published, only the manuscript survives
In 1868, after the discovery of a manuscript copy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The whole treatise remained unpublished during Grotius's lifetime; only chapter XII, Mare liberum, appeared in 1609. The complete text was not published until 1868, after the discovery of a manuscript copy.
